documents.unit: Center for Innovation in Teaching & Learning (CITL)
documents.title: Integrate AI into your Teaching
documents.summary: CITL's campus teaching guidance frames generative AI as transformative and urges faculty to engage with it, listing benefits for faculty (drafting materials) and students (tutoring, study aids, writing help). It gives ethical guidance on integrity, accuracy, privacy, access and IP, advises against blanket syllabus bans in favor of explaining when AI is acceptable, and suggests assignment makeovers. It leaves course rules to instructors.

units.anchor: Faculty, staff, and students cannot afford to ignore this shift
Faculty can model curiosity and adaptability by engaging with Generative AI
units.policy: Faculty can model curiosity and adaptability by engaging with generative AI and showing students how to navigate uncertainty with rigor and creativity.

units.anchor: AI literacy is essential for future success because employers are expecting graduates
units.policy: For students, AI literacy is essential for future success because employers expect graduates to understand and use AI tools responsibly.

units.anchor: Our challenge is to harness the benefits of AI while keeping higher education deeply human
units.policy: The efficiency and innovation AI provides must be balanced by human imagination, empathy, and critical thought; the challenge is to harness AI's benefits while keeping higher education deeply human.

units.anchor: traditional teaching methods must be re-examined in light of new possibilities
instructors need to understand not only how to use AI effectively for their own work
units.policy: Instructors need to understand how to use AI effectively for their own work and how to weave it into their teaching, to prepare students for a workforce where AI literacy is essential.

units.anchor: Instructors can use AI to create the first draft of a course syllabus
units.policy: Instructors can use AI to create first drafts of a course syllabus, assignment and discussion prompts, and grading rubrics, which with necessary revisions can save hours of work.
units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor use of AI for teaching work

units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor use of AI for teaching work

units.anchor: gives them more time for higher-level teaching activities like mentoring
units.policy: Using AI for some course and teaching tasks gives faculty more time for higher-level teaching such as mentoring, in-depth discussion, and fostering student engagement.
units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor use of AI for teaching work

units.anchor: Instructor guidance is needed to help students use AI tools for course learning activities
units.policy: Instructor guidance is needed to help students use AI tools for course learning activities and assignments.

units.anchor: students can use AI tools independently to support their learning
a tutor generating study aids such as flashcards, quizzes, and practice questions
units.policy: AI can serve as a tutor generating study aids such as flashcards, quizzes, and practice questions to help students test and strengthen their knowledge.

units.anchor: AI tools can serve as a personal teaching assistant, explaining complex ideas
units.policy: AI tools can serve as a personal teaching assistant, explaining complex ideas that are difficult to understand.

units.anchor: AI can help students with outlining, idea generation, and deeper engagement with concepts
serve as a writing tutor by shortening over-long text, improving spelling and grammar
units.policy: AI can serve as a writing tutor by shortening over-long text, improving spelling and grammar, and bringing more clarity to students' ideas.

units.anchor: use AI in ways that support their learning, without replacing the real work of learning
units.policy: Instructors can help students understand how to use AI in ways that support their learning without replacing the real work of learning how to learn.

units.anchor: faculty should be aware of ethical considerations and instruct their students
units.policy: Faculty should be aware of ethical considerations and instruct their students on how to use AI responsibly.

units.anchor: Define clear boundaries for AI use in course assignments and assessments.
units.policy: Instructors should define clear boundaries for AI use in course assignments and assessments.

units.anchor: Remind students that AI-generated text and ideas must be cited appropriately.
Help students understand why academic integrity standards exist, and how they should use AI
units.policy: Instructors should help students understand why academic integrity standards exist and how to use AI to support rather than hinder their learning.

units.anchor: AI outputs can be inaccurate, biased, or completely fabricated.
help students to develop critical thinking skills and to practice evaluating AI-generated content responsibly
units.policy: Instructors should help students develop critical thinking skills and practice evaluating AI-generated content responsibly.

units.anchor: they must be vigilant in preserving FERPA data and student privacy
units.policy: Because AI is continually collecting user information, faculty must be vigilant in preserving FERPA data and student privacy.

units.anchor: Faculty and students are encouraged to use campus-approved AI tools
never share sensitive, or proprietary information with third-party tools that may expose them
units.policy: Faculty and students should never share sensitive or proprietary information with third-party tools that may expose them to security risks.

units.anchor: Faculty should ensure that all students can access digital tools if assignments require them.
group projects or shared resources can help minimize access and disparity issues
Faculty should also be aware that some digital tools may not be accessible.
Follow campus guidelines and recommend campus-approved AI tools whenever possible.
units.policy: Faculty should follow campus guidelines and recommend campus-approved AI tools whenever possible.

units.anchor: Faculty have a responsibility to uphold the ethical, professional, and intellectual property standards
units.policy: Faculty have a responsibility to uphold the ethical, professional, and intellectual property standards expected of university researchers and educators, and to impress these standards on their students.

units.anchor: AI tools are always collecting personal and proprietary information during interactive or conversational use
many tools may fail to comply with laws and regulations governing data and content use
can act as an idea partner to quickly draft learning outcomes, grading rubrics, slide decks
units.policy: Campus tools like Copilot, Gemini, or Chat GPT EDU can act as an idea partner for instructors to quickly draft learning outcomes, grading rubrics, slide decks, or suggestions for in-class activities.
units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor use of AI for teaching work

units.anchor: add a blanket AI policy to your syllabus, but this is not advised
units.policy: Adding a blanket AI policy to the syllabus is a knee-jerk response that is not advised.

units.anchor: try to explain how and when it will be ok to use AI in class
units.policy: Instead of a blanket policy, instructors should try to explain how and when it will be OK to use AI in class.

units.anchor: demonstrating key benefits and limitations of AI and show how AI writing differs
units.policy: Instructors should demonstrate key benefits and limitations of AI and show how AI writing differs from natural writing.

units.anchor: Modify a few assignments so students can explore using AI tools in limited ways
units.policy: Instructors should modify a few assignments so students can explore using AI tools in limited ways, such as for brainstorming or revision.

units.anchor: Discuss how AI can support student learning without replacing the work of learning.
units.policy: Instructors should discuss how AI can support student learning without replacing the work of learning.

units.policy: Building specific examples into the course makes it easier to create syllabus language that defines the parameters for course work and assignments while still giving students opportunities to explore AI tools.

units.anchor: rethink some of your assignments and consider how you are assessing student learning
units.policy: Instructors should rethink some assignments and consider how they are assessing student learning in light of AI.

units.anchor: less about catching out students who are using AI to do their assignments
units.policy: The goal of assignment makeovers is less about catching students who use AI to do their assignments and more about creating learning activities that engage students more deeply.

units.anchor: Require students to make short informational presentations in class, alone, or in small groups.
Ask students to engage in classroom role play exercises, debates, and panel discussions
Ask students to show what they know by working alone or in groups.
units.policy: To make learning visible, instructors should ask students to show what they know (e.g., concept maps, diagrams, timelines) working alone or in groups.

units.anchor: Ask students to create short podcasts, infographics, digital storybooks or graphic novels.
CITL staff can help you design learning activities and assignments customized for your course content.
CITL invites faculty and students to engage with us as we learn more about AI
units.policy: CITL invites faculty and students to engage with it as it learns more about AI, demystifies it, and makes it a helpful partner.

documents.title: AI Guidance: Sample Statements for Engineering
tiers: Use When Instructed to Do So
documents.summary: Grainger College of Engineering's AI guidance page offers four template syllabus statements for engineering courses (Restricted, Limited Use, Use When Instructed, All Use) for instructors to adopt. It also reproduces example statements from CS 411 (assignment-specific prohibition vs. allowed-with-attribution) and a Northern Illinois University writing statement. The college itself sets no single rule.

units.anchor: Template Statements for Engineering
units.policy: The college provides template syllabus statements for engineering at four levels: Restricted, Limited Use, Use When Instructed to Do So, and All Use.

units.anchor: are not permitted for any stage or phase of work in this class
units.policy: (Restricted template) Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Co-pilot, and Gemini are not permitted for any stage or phase of work in the class.

units.anchor: will be considered academic dishonesty and a violation of the University of Illinois Student Code
units.policy: (Restricted template) Use of generative AI tools in the course is considered academic dishonesty and a violation of the University of Illinois Student Code.

units.anchor: Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by artificial intelligence (AI) is considered plagiarism
units.policy: (Restricted template) Any work written, developed, created, or inspired by AI is considered plagiarism and will not be tolerated.

units.anchor: for this class their use hinders the learning process and therefore is not allowed
units.policy: (Restricted template) While AI tools will find their place in workforces and personal lives, in this class their use hinders the learning process and therefore is not allowed.

units.anchor: The appropriate use of generative AI varies from course to course.
there are times when generative AI may be useful in the course
units.policy: (Limited Use template) There are times when generative AI may be useful in the course.

units.anchor: you must document and attribute all AI contributions to your coursework
units.policy: (Limited Use template) Students who use generative AI as permitted must document and attribute all AI contributions to their coursework.

units.anchor: take full responsibility for the contributions including the accuracy of the information
units.policy: (Limited Use template) Students must take full responsibility for AI contributions, including the accuracy of the information and reliability of sources.

units.anchor: keep a journal documenting prompts, AI responses, and your usage
units.policy: (Limited Use template) When using generative AI, students must keep a journal documenting prompts, AI responses, and their usage.

units.anchor: Your instructor may ask you to provide this documentation.
units.policy: (Limited Use template) The instructor may ask students to provide their AI usage journal.

units.anchor: Add acceptable uses here

units.anchor: Add unacceptable uses here
units.policy: (Limited Use template) Instructors list the uses of generative AI students may not make in their course.

units.anchor: If you have a question about the use of Generative AI, please reach out
units.policy: (Limited Use template) Students with a question about the use of generative AI should reach out to their instructors.

units.anchor: Failure to abide by these guidelines is a violation of academic integrity.
units.policy: (Limited Use template) Failure to abide by the course's AI guidelines is a violation of academic integrity.

units.anchor: We will investigate suspected uses of generative AI that do not follow these guidelines
units.policy: (Limited Use template) Instructors will investigate suspected uses of generative AI that do not follow the guidelines and apply sanctions as outlined in the University of Illinois Student Code.

units.anchor: During our class, we may use AI tools such as ChatGPT.
units.policy: (Use When Instructed template) During class, AI tools such as ChatGPT may be used.

units.anchor: You will be informed as to when, where, and how these tools are permitted
units.policy: (Use When Instructed template) Students will be informed when, where, and how AI tools are permitted, along with guidance for attribution.

units.anchor: Any use outside of when permission is explicitly given will be considered academic dishonesty
units.policy: (Use When Instructed template) Any AI use outside of when permission is explicitly given is considered academic dishonesty and a violation of the University of Illinois Student Code.

units.anchor: Generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Co-pilot, and Gemini are welcome in this class
units.policy: (All Use template) Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Co-pilot, and Gemini are welcome in the class.

units.anchor: provided that you cite when and how you use the tool
units.policy: (All Use template) Students must cite when and how they use generative AI tools.

units.policy: (All Use template) Students will be provided with examples of how to cite their use of AI tools for assignments.

units.anchor: AI programs are not a replacement for critical thinking, analysis, creativity, originality, and problem-solving.
Engineering is a craft that you must develop over time by learning skills

documents.title: Using AI
documents.summary: Grainger's 'Using AI' page frames appropriate use as augmenting rather than replacing human thinking and gives examples of appropriate uses (proofreading, generating course materials, example datasets, translation, format conversion, tutoring) and inappropriate ones. Much of it addresses instructors (grading, letters, emails, peer review) and data privacy/FERPA, and it sets no course-level rule.

units.anchor: leveraging AI as a supportive tool rather than a substitute for human intellect
If the intention of using AI is to augment human thinking, then it is likely
units.policy: If the intention of using AI is to augment human thinking, it is likely an appropriate use of AI.

units.policy: If the intention of using AI is to replace human thinking, it is likely an inappropriate use of AI.

units.policy: By tailoring prompts, AI can help learners practice, solve problems step by step, and receive feedback.

units.policy: Especially for English Language Learners, it is a good idea for students to use AI as a proofreader first.

units.policy: While AI can sometimes replace a writer's words and alter their style, it excels at correcting structure and grammar.

units.policy: AI can assist in translating text between languages, often better than Google Translate, e.g., for documents such as letters of recommendation written in other languages.

units.policy: When asking an LLM to convert formats, it is helpful to give it an example of the before and after.

units.policy: It is usually very effective to copy in the text of a homework set and prompt the LLM to generate a new set of similar difficulty and content for more practice.

units.policy: For tutoring, a learner can prompt AI to generate a problem and help them solve it on their own using the Socratic method, never giving the answer but giving feedback on the next step.

units.policy: Anything uploaded to AI could be used to train it, and data-safety guarantees cannot be verified, which has implications for FERPA-protected information.

units.policy: AI saves us from having to spend time thinking about things, but sometimes that thinking is precisely what we are supposed to be doing.

units.policy: Using an LLM to summarize a paper to get a high-level idea of its content can be helpful, e.g., in deciding whether to read it.

units.policy: Copy-pasting an AI-generated summary as the concluding paragraph of a paper you have written could be problematic.

units.policy: AI might produce text in perfect English, but it often produces over-generic text less useful for a reader.

documents.unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
documents.title: AI in CS 124
documents.summary: CS 124's AI statement explains why the course has embraced AI coding agents: it is the future of software development, earlier experiments with AI on traditional specs failed, and the independent project is now built around Claude Code. AI is expected on the project, prohibited on proctored CBTF quizzes (60% of the grade), and students must validate AI code by testing. An FAQ covers scope, cost ($40-60), cheating, and why human partners are not allowed.

units.anchor: CS 124 has embraced AI coding agents to prepare students for the future of programming.
Properly used, it acts as a multiplier
units.policy: Properly used, generative AI acts as a multiplier: changes that took hours can be done in minutes, projects that took weeks in days.

units.anchor: This is the future of software development.
units.policy: CS 124 embraces AI mainly because it is the future of software development.

units.anchor: We're preparing students today for the programming of today.
neglecting to teach students how to use them effectively would be wrong
units.policy: Pretending new AI approaches don't exist or neglecting to teach students how to use them effectively would be wrong.

units.anchor: Employers expect graduates to know these skills.
the ability of AI to generate entire apps from human-language specifications is tremendously important
units.policy: Because 80% of CS 124 students are non-majors, AI's ability to generate entire apps from human-language specifications is tremendously important and increases the value of the basic programming skills taught.

units.anchor: students can complete fun and high-impact independent projects along the way
units.policy: Getting started with generative AI will ensure students can complete fun and high-impact independent projects along the way.

units.anchor: we began allowing students to use AI on the course project as an experiment
units.policy: In Fall 2024, the course began allowing students to use AI on the course project as an experiment.

units.anchor: tested whether Claude could complete the Fall 2025 project from test suites alone
units.policy: The instructor tested whether Claude could complete the Fall 2025 project from test suites alone, and it could, with minimal human intervention.

units.anchor: keeping the same project structure while allowing AI. But this approach didn't work.
units.policy: In Fall 2025, keeping the same project structure while allowing AI was tried as a compromise, and it did not work.

units.anchor: AI coding agents have become too good at this translation step
units.policy: AI coding agents have become too good at translating specifications to code, and the tension between precise specifications (needed for fair automated grading) and imprecise ones (needed to prevent AI doing all the work) proved irreconcilable.

units.anchor: Some students used AI to complete almost all the work without learning much
units.policy: Some students used AI to complete almost all the work without learning much in the process.

units.anchor: the valuable human contribution is formulating the idea and specification itself
units.policy: If AI handles translation from specification to code, the valuable human contribution is formulating the idea and specification itself, which the independent project is designed to teach.

units.anchor: introduces students to how to use the most capable AI programming tools: coding agents
units.policy: CS 124 introduces students to how to use the most capable AI programming tools: coding agents.

units.anchor: conversational programming requires creativity, planning, and critical thinking
units.policy: Conversational programming with AI agents requires creativity, planning, and critical thinking, even if natural language avoids many syntactic challenges.

units.anchor: keep our AI agents on a leash
units.policy: AI agents should be kept on a leash.

units.anchor: we must always understand the software AI helps us create
each student designs and builds something of their own, working with AI coding agents throughout
units.policy: Starting Spring 2026, in My Project each student designs and builds something of their own, working with AI coding agents throughout the process.

units.anchor: We'll discuss effective prompting strategies, understanding AI-generated changes, validating code through automated testing
units.policy: The course discusses effective prompting strategies, understanding AI-generated changes, validating code through automated testing, and redirecting AI when it gets off track.

units.anchor: the old model—where students receive a detailed specification, translate it to code, and submit—is broken
units.policy: The old model where students receive a detailed specification, translate it to code, and submit is broken in the age of AI coding agents.

units.anchor: coming up with good problems to solve and describing solutions in a form
units.policy: The independent project gives students practice coming up with good problems to solve and describing solutions in a form agents can use.

units.anchor: Writing clear, effective prompts for coding tasks
units.policy: A learning objective for AI-supported programming is writing clear, effective prompts for coding tasks.

units.anchor: Validating AI-generated code through automated testing
units.policy: A learning objective for AI-supported programming is validating AI-generated code through automated testing.

units.anchor: Writing effective test cases
units.policy: A learning objective for AI-supported programming is writing effective test cases.

units.anchor: Recognizing when AI is going off-track and redirecting it
units.policy: A learning objective for AI-supported programming is recognizing when AI is going off-track and redirecting it.

units.anchor: Balancing AI assistance with personal understanding
units.policy: A learning objective for AI-supported programming is balancing AI assistance with personal understanding.

units.anchor: inspired and guided by our own usage of these tools
units.policy: The course's teaching about generative AI is inspired and guided by the instructors' own usage of these tools.

units.anchor: Geoff is actively collaborating with Claude Code on the many pieces of CS 124 courseware
units.policy: The instructor actively collaborates with Claude Code on the many pieces of CS 124 courseware he maintains.

units.anchor: We don't simply hand students an AI tool and tell them to build something.
units.policy: Students are not simply handed an AI tool; the independent project includes a carefully scaffolded sequence of activities from idea to working app.

units.anchor: build quick prototypes on claude.ai, try each other's, critique them, and revise their own
units.policy: Students build quick prototypes on claude.ai, try each other's, critique them, and revise their own.

units.anchor: they create a repository, connect Claude Code to it, and start building from their prototype
weekly project workshops have students pairing up, critiquing each other's work
units.policy: Weekly project workshops have students pairing up, critiquing each other's work, and deciding what to do next, with a project mentor at every table.

units.anchor: being able to teach both classical programming and conversational programming
units.policy: Access to a computer-based testing facility lets CS 124 teach both classical programming and conversational programming.

units.anchor: it is still critical that users develop and maintain classical programming abilities—writing code by hand
writing it by hand builds the habits of mind that make you a better collaborator
units.policy: Writing code by hand builds habits of mind that make students better collaborators with AI: precision about specifications, anticipating failure, tracing data, and judging correctness.

units.anchor: continue to develop these skills through our daily lessons, homework, and particularly the weekly quizzes
units.policy: CS 124 will continue to develop classical programming skills through daily lessons, homework, and particularly the weekly quizzes.

units.anchor: We will continue to prohibit AI use on our proctored quizzes
units.policy: AI use is prohibited on proctored quizzes given in the CBTF.

units.anchor: Every quiz includes programming and debugging challenges, which must be completed without access to AI.
At some point in the future we may add prompting challenges to the quizzes
The proctored quizzes carry 60% of a student's grade.
we will continue to monitor student performance in CS 124 and in later courses
units.policy: The course will continue to monitor student performance in CS 124 and later courses and adjust as needed to ensure it still effectively teaches classical programming.

units.anchor: CS 124 only teaches AI-supported programming on the independent project.
students need explicit instruction on how to work with AI effectively
units.policy: Simply allowing AI on a traditional project was not enough; students need explicit instruction on how to work with AI effectively.

units.anchor: the project itself needs to be designed around AI collaboration
reasons to be concerned about the rise of AI: safety, human autonomy, job loss
units.policy: There are many legitimate reasons to be concerned about the rise of AI: safety, human autonomy, job loss, ethical concerns, and other issues.

units.anchor: We encourage CS 124 students to engage with these issues in conversation with each other
units.policy: CS 124 students are encouraged to engage with concerns about AI in conversation with each other and with course staff.

units.anchor: we should not lose sight of the fact that these developments are tremendously exciting
Knowledge of specific language, syntax, and frameworks—code—is no longer a bottleneck.
units.policy: (Quoting Kailash Nadh) Knowledge of specific language, syntax, and frameworks is no longer a bottleneck; critical thinking and foundational human skills matter most.

documents.unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
documents.title: CS 128 Syllabus (AI Policy)
documents.summary: CS 128's syllabus makes AI optional and permits it to support the process (understanding problems, planning, concepts, error messages, reviewing one's own code, test design) but never to produce submitted code; vibe coding is an integrity violation and students must explain every line. Every AI-assisted assignment requires an AI Usage Reflection Form plus complete transcripts; quizzes are AI-free in the CBTF, code interviews check understanding, and first/second-offense sanctions are stated.

units.anchor: no collaboration is permitted, no AI tool may be used
units.policy: Every quiz is taken in the CBTF under proctored conditions and completed entirely on one's own; no AI tool may be used.

units.anchor: Attempting to circumvent those conditions is an academic integrity violation
units.policy: Attempting to circumvent quiz conditions is an academic integrity violation referred to the FAIR process.

units.anchor: AI tools may be used only in accordance with the AI Policy
units.policy: On machine problems, graded lessons, and recitation, AI tools may be used only in accordance with the AI Policy.

units.anchor: we select some students for a one-on-one session with the staff
units.policy: After each MP, some students are selected for a one-on-one code interview with staff in which they explain the code they submitted.

units.anchor: choose you on the basis of your submission history
units.policy: Students may be chosen for code interviews at random or based on submission history, academic integrity concerns, or other factors.

units.anchor: You are responsible for being able to explain any solution you submitted for the MP
You must reply to the code interview invitation by email within 48 hours
units.policy: Students must reply to a code interview invitation within 48 hours; failing to do so results in a zero on the MP.

units.anchor: explain your code to the staff's satisfaction
units.policy: Students must explain their code to the staff's satisfaction: what it does, the design decisions behind it, and why each language feature was used.

units.anchor: you forfeit the grade for that MP, independent of the correctness of the code
units.policy: A student who cannot explain their code in the interview forfeits the grade for that MP, regardless of code correctness.

units.anchor: Our assessment of your explanation is final and not open to review.
any generative system that produces code, text, or explanations in response to a prompt
units.policy: An AI tool is any generative system that produces code, text, or explanations in response to a prompt, however accessed: chat interface, editor extension, command-line tool, or agent.

units.anchor: non-generative editor completion are not AI tools under this policy and are always permitted
units.policy: Dictionaries, translation tools, spell checkers, and non-generative editor completion are not AI tools under the policy and are always permitted.

units.anchor: no tool beyond what the testing environment provides falls within any permitted use
units.policy: During a quiz, no tool beyond what the testing environment provides is permitted.

units.anchor: Using AI in this course is optional.
units.policy: Using AI in the course is optional; every assignment can be completed for full marks without AI.

units.anchor: you must write your own code
you must be able to explain every line of it
you should be able to answer immediately and confidently, without consulting any resource
units.policy: If a staff member asks why a line was written, what a variable represents, or how code works, students should be able to answer immediately and confidently without consulting any resource.

units.anchor: you have not yet learned what the assignment was designed to teach
units.policy: If a student cannot explain their code, they have not learned what the assignment was designed to teach, even if the code compiles and passes tests.

units.anchor: AI may support your process
units.policy: AI may support the student's process, e.g., understanding the problem, learning concepts, developing a strategy, debugging attempts, and verifying correctness.

units.anchor: it may not produce your product, i.e., the code you submit
which you must be able to reproduce independently
units.policy: Students must be able to reproduce the code they submit independently.

units.anchor: Ask the AI to help you understand what an assignment is asking
units.policy: Students may ask AI to help them understand what an assignment is asking, identify its component parts, and clarify ambiguous requirements.

units.anchor: Use the AI to help you formulate a high-level approach before you begin writing code
units.policy: Students may use AI to help formulate a high-level approach before writing code: discussing strategies, edge cases, and logical structure.

units.anchor: When you encounter unfamiliar C++ constructs, language features, or programming concepts, use the AI
units.policy: Students may use AI to help make sense of unfamiliar C++ constructs, language features, or programming concepts.

units.anchor: The AI can help you interpret what went wrong and why.
units.policy: Students may use AI to help interpret compiler errors and runtime failures.

units.anchor: After you have written code yourself, use the AI to help you
units.policy: After writing code themselves, students may use AI to help check whether the implementation aligns with their intent and identify potential issues.

units.anchor: Work with the AI to identify the scenarios, boundary conditions, and
units.policy: Students may work with AI to identify the scenarios, boundary conditions, and expected behavior their tests should cover.

units.policy: Where the evidence shows a violation is more probable than not, the course files a FAIR case.

units.anchor: Use an AI tool in any way not permitted by the AI Policy
units.policy: Using an AI tool in any way not permitted by the AI Policy is cheating.

units.anchor: Use an AI tool without submitting the corresponding AI Usage Reflection Form and transcript.
units.policy: Using an AI tool without submitting the corresponding AI Usage Reflection Form and transcript is cheating.

units.anchor: including to another person and to any AI tool
units.policy: Students may not reveal, discuss, or enter quiz or other private assessment content anywhere outside the testing environment, including to any AI tool, even after the quiz window closes.

units.anchor: If you are ever uncertain about what is allowed, seek clarification from the instructor
units.policy: Students uncertain about what is allowed should seek clarification from the instructor via the forum before using an AI tool.

units.anchor: A reduction of one full letter grade in the class
units.policy: A first offense brings a one-letter-grade reduction in the class and a zero on each assessment involved.

units.anchor: Second offense, or an extreme act affecting other students
units.policy: A second offense, or an extreme act affecting other students, results in an F in the course.

units.anchor: These sanctions are more severe than the departmental recommendations, and we apply them in full.

documents.unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
documents.title: CS 225 Collaboration & Academic Integrity (AI Coding Tools (Generative AI) Policy)
documents.summary: CS 225's integrity page bans AI tools of any kind unless an assignment directly states otherwise, arguing that AI teaches less than students think, is like using a friend's solution, and leaves students unprepared for AI-free exams. It notes plagiarism checking, holds that AI should be taught after foundations are built, and lists general sanctions (zero on MP, zero on exam, escalating penalties).

units.anchor: CS 225 does not permit the use of AI tools of any kind
units.policy: Unless directly stated in an assignment, CS 225 does not permit the use of AI tools of any kind.

units.anchor: in practice it often teaches you far less than you realize
units.policy: Using AI tools, though it may seem supplemental, often teaches students far less than they realize; assignments are structured to teach important concepts and skills.

units.anchor: generative AI is akin to having access to 'a friend's solution'
your code is checked for plagiarism and that multiple students relying on the same tools
units.policy: Code is checked for plagiarism, and multiple students relying on the same AI tools will often produce very similar solutions.

units.anchor: such tools are not allowed during the exam setting
an over-reliance on such tools can leave you struggling to code independently on exams
units.policy: Over-reliance on AI tools can leave students struggling to code independently on exams or retaining less knowledge for future classes.

units.anchor: practicing fundamental skills imparts knowledge in a way that immediately receiving the answer does not
units.policy: Like learning arithmetic despite calculators, practicing fundamental skills imparts knowledge in a way that immediately receiving the answer does not.

units.anchor: AI tools should be taught after you have already established strong foundational skills
units.policy: The course staff's view is that AI tools should be taught after students have established strong foundational skills, not as an alternative to building them.

units.anchor: infraction of academic integrity on an MP will result in a 0 on that MP
units.policy: Any academic integrity infraction on an MP results in a 0 on that MP, regardless of when the student is notified.

units.anchor: The penalty for cheating on an exam is an automatic zero on the exam.
Repeated violations may result in cumulative and increasingly severe additional penalties.
units.policy: Repeated violations may bring cumulative, increasingly severe penalties, such as a letter grade drop, loss of extra credit, or a failing grade.

units.anchor: every violation of academic integrity will be reported to the department
units.policy: Every academic integrity violation is reported to the department and becomes part of the student's permanent record.

documents.unit: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
documents.title: ECE 220 Fall 2026 course page (Syllabus: Use of generative AI)
documents.summary: ECE 220's syllabus strongly discourages generative AI for solving MPs because the course's goal is mastery of basic programming paradigms and low-level implementation, but it does not ban it and staff will not actively police it. It warns that reliance on AI disadvantages students on device-free exams and quizzes and tells students to ask the instructor if unsure.

units.anchor: are now routinely capable of solving advanced programming questions
units.policy: Generative AI like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude is now routinely capable of solving advanced programming questions.

units.anchor: The fundamental learning objective in this course is mastery of the basic programming paradigms
units.policy: The fundamental learning objective is mastery of basic programming paradigms, algorithms, data structures, and their low-level implementations.

units.anchor: Use of generative AI for solving MPs is STRONGLY DISCOURAGED.
use generative AI as a crutch, it is likely you will not master these concepts
units.policy: Students who use generative AI as a crutch are likely not to master the course concepts.

units.anchor: Our staff will not actively police your use of generative AI
if you rely on them too much, you may find yourself at a disadvantage
units.policy: Relying on AI too much may leave students at a disadvantage on exams and quizzes.

units.anchor: the exams and quizzes where you will not have access to such tools
units.policy: Students do not have access to generative AI tools on exams and quizzes.

units.anchor: Neither electronic nor mechanical devices are permitted while taking the exams or quizzes
units.policy: Neither electronic nor mechanical devices are permitted during exams or quizzes, except those medically necessary.

units.anchor: If you are confused about what exactly is or is not permitted, you should ask
units.policy: Students confused about what is permitted should ask the instructor for clarification.

units.anchor: Confusion or ignorance of the rules is not an excuse.

documents.unit: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
documents.title: ECE 391 Fall 2026 course page (AI Policy)
documents.summary: ECE 391 lists permitted resources and explicitly prohibits AI tools and AI-enabled IDEs; AI may not be used in any way without written instructor permission, and VS Code may be used only with all AI extensions disabled. For group work, any member's AI use makes the whole team liable, members must police each other, and violations bring no credit plus a 10-point course grade drop.

units.anchor: You are not allowed to use any resource that does not fall into one
units.policy: Students may not use any resource outside the listed permitted categories unless they have explicit instructor permission.

units.anchor: Any code you did not write yourself
units.policy: Students are prohibited from using any code they did not write themselves, except code provided by the course.

units.anchor: AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Co-Pilot
units.policy: Students are explicitly prohibited from using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Co-Pilot.

units.anchor: IDEs with AI functionality (see below).
units.policy: Students are explicitly prohibited from using IDEs with AI functionality.

units.anchor: You are not permitted to use AI in any way unless explicitly permitted in writing
units.policy: Students are not permitted to use AI in any way unless explicitly permitted in writing by the instructors.

units.anchor: Visual Studio Code, which must be used with all AI extensions disabled
units.policy: Without written permission, students may not use any IDE with AI functions, except Visual Studio Code with all AI extensions disabled.

units.anchor: Prohibited IDEs include (but are not limited to): Google Antigravity, Cursor, Trae, Windsurf, Zed AI.
The Microsoft C/C++ IntelliSense extension is permitted (but not IntelliCode)
your own individual work for individual assignments and the work of your team
units.policy: All work products must be the student's own individual work (or the team's for group assignments) and completed using permitted resources only.

units.anchor: Use of AI by any team member will result in an academic integrity violation
units.policy: Use of AI by any team member results in an academic integrity violation for the entire team.

units.anchor: take proactive steps to make sure that other members of your group complete work
units.policy: Students must take proactive steps to ensure other group members complete work in accordance with course policies, including AI policies.

units.anchor: If you suspect one of your team members of violating a course policy, report this
units.policy: Students who suspect a team member of violating a course policy must report it to course staff immediately.

units.anchor: all members are collectively responsible for adherence to this policy
units.policy: For team-based assessments, all members are collectively responsible for adherence to the policy.

units.anchor: Academic integrity violations will be processed through the FAIR system
you will receive no credit on the assignment and a 10 percentage point
units.policy: An academic integrity violation on an assignment brings no credit on the assignment and a 10-percentage-point drop in the course grade.

units.anchor: If you cheat on an exam, you will receive no credit on the exam
units.policy: Cheating on an exam brings no credit on the exam and a 10-percentage-point drop in the course grade.

documents.title: Syllabus | IS445 - Data Viz - BCU (Policy on ChatGPT and other LLMs)
documents.summary: IS 445's LLM policy allows ChatGPT-like tools only for brainstorming, inspiration, expanding ideas, and improving writing, never as the primary source of answers, and forbids pasting assignment questions into an LLM. Students must verify LLM output, cite the model, date, and prompt, give a validation plan or validation tests, and mark AI-generated sections; the policy itself was drafted with ChatGPT and adapted by instructors.

units.anchor: learn how to validate statements and code or software
units.policy: Written and programming assignments are for students to apply what they learned and learn how to validate statements and code, not to produce perfect text or code.

units.anchor: we want to see how you problem-solve and what you think about a particular topic
useful for getting ideas about how to phrase text or to get started
units.policy: LLMs can be useful for getting ideas about how to phrase text or to get started on a coding/software problem.

units.anchor: they are not meant to be used in place of your critical thinking skills
units.policy: LLMs are not meant to be used in place of students' critical thinking skills.

units.anchor: we hear your thoughts on topics than it is to generate 100% perfect English
units.policy: It is more important that instructors hear students' thoughts than that students generate 100% perfect English.

units.anchor: if you make use of LLMS, we expect significant extra work to be submitted
units.policy: Students who use LLMs are expected to submit significant extra work with their submissions.

units.anchor: allowed to utilize ChatGPT or similar AI language models for course assignments or tests
units.policy: Students are allowed to use ChatGPT or similar AI language models for course assignments or tests, but only in specific situations.

units.anchor: Such usage should be restricted to brainstorming, seeking inspiration, expanding ideas, and improving writing
must not constitute the primary source of content or answers
units.policy: LLM usage must not constitute the primary source of content or answers.

units.anchor: You cannot copy full-text of assignment questions and input directly into an LLM
units.policy: Copying the full text of assignment questions into an LLM is not allowed and is plagiarism.

units.anchor: Students must not directly copy or paraphrase AI-generated text without proper attribution.
to directly answer specific questions or complete entire assignments is strictly prohibited
units.policy: Using ChatGPT or similar models to directly answer specific questions or complete entire assignments is strictly prohibited.

units.anchor: Students should rely on their knowledge and understanding, supplemented by AI tools for assistance.
Students must critically assess and verify any information obtained through ChatGPT or similar AI
units.policy: Students must critically assess and verify any information obtained through ChatGPT or similar models before incorporating it into their work.

units.anchor: Misleading or inaccurate information from the AI model should not be used in their submissions.
Cross-reference the AI-generated information with reputable sources to verify its accuracy and reliability.
units.policy: Students must cross-reference AI-generated information with reputable sources to verify its accuracy and reliability.

units.anchor: Include the LLM name and date of usage
units.policy: Students who use an LLM must include the LLM name and date of usage.

units.anchor: Include the prompt used
units.policy: Students who use an LLM must include the prompt used.

units.anchor: validation plan
units.policy: Students who use an LLM must include a 'validation plan' for each statement they use from it.

units.anchor: links to research supporting this claim need to be included
units.policy: For writing, LLM-output statements must be supported by links to research, and any LLM-generated links must each be verified.

units.anchor: you will need to create your own validation tests to run the code
units.policy: For code, students must create their own validation tests for LLM code and describe in a few sentences how the tests relate to the prompt.

units.anchor: Clearly indicate any sections or contents that are AI-generated.
units.policy: Students must clearly indicate any sections or contents that are AI-generated.

units.anchor: Each assignment or test may have specific instructions regarding the use of AI tools
units.policy: Each assignment or test may have specific AI-use instructions, which students must carefully review and comply with.

units.anchor: will be treated as an academic integrity breach and subject to disciplinary action
units.policy: Violating the class policy on ChatGPT use is treated as an academic integrity breach subject to disciplinary action per institutional guidelines.

units.anchor: were generated by ChatGPT, and selected, modified, and adapted by Dr. Koh
units.policy: The class AI policy was generated by ChatGPT and selected, modified, and adapted by the instructors.

units.anchor: The used prompts include: Give me class policy on the use of ChatGPT
units.policy: The instructors disclose the prompts used to generate the class AI policy.

new_types.name: Instructor use of AI for teaching work
new_types.definition: What instructors or staff may, should, or should not use AI for in their own teaching and professional work (drafting syllabi, assignments, rubrics, quiz items, example datasets, course logistics, translation, recommendation letters, student emails, peer review). Excludes grading (P46) and disclosure of instructor use or AI-made materials (P47/P48).

notes: Coder B. Testimonial quotes on the CITL page (faculty/student voices) were treated as illustrations and not coded. Long example prompts and the autonomous-vehicle lesson examples on Grainger/CITL pages were not coded as separate units. CS 124 syllabus and CS 128 syllabus: only AI-related passages plus the general integrity sanctions that govern AI misuse were coded; non-AI collaboration, attendance, accommodation and wellbeing boilerplate was skipped. Template statements and example course statements embedded in the Grainger guidance page were coded as units of that document (prefixed by template/course in the policy text). ECE 220 stance coded 'permit' because AI is strongly discouraged but not prohibited (no 'discourage' stance exists).
